stem: A 58-year-old woman with seropositive rheumatoid arthritis presents with a three-day history of a severely painful left eye. She describes the pain as deep and boring. On examination, the eye is diffusely red with associated photophobia and slightly blurred vision. Simple analgesia has provided no relief. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Scleritis
Scleritis is the correct diagnosis. This patient presents with the classic features of scleritis: a severe, deep, boring pain in the eye, diffuse redness (scleral injection), photophobia, and a reduction in visual acuity. The key diagnostic clue is the strong association between scleritis and systemic autoimmune conditions, with rheumatoid arthritis being the most common, occurring in up to 50% of cases of non-infectious scleritis. The severity of the pain, which is often poorly responsive to simple analgesia and can wake the patient from sleep, is a hallmark feature that distinguishes it from more benign causes of a red eye. Scleritis represents a full-thickness inflammation of the sclera and can be sight-threatening if not managed promptly. Urgent referral to an ophthalmologist is mandatory for confirmation of diagnosis and initiation of treatment, which typically involves systemic NSAIDs, corticosteroids, or other immunosuppressive agents.

Episcleritis
Episcleritis is an important differential. It involves inflammation of the superficial episcleral tissue. While it is also associated with rheumatoid arthritis, it typically presents with mild discomfort or a gritty sensation rather than the severe, deep pain described in this scenario. The redness in episcleritis is often sectoral (affecting only a segment of the eye) rather than diffuse, and it does not typically affect vision. The blood vessels in episcleritis will blanch with the application of topical phenylephrine, whereas the deeper vessels in scleritis will not, although this test is performed in a specialist setting.

Acute anterior uveitis
Acute anterior uveitis presents with a painful red eye, photophobia, and blurred vision. However, the pain is often described as aching, and characteristic signs include a ciliary flush (a ring of redness around the cornea) and a small, poorly reactive pupil. While uveitis can be associated with systemic inflammatory diseases, it is more classically linked with seronegative spondyloarthropathies (e.g., ankylosing spondylitis) and sarcoidosis, rather than rheumatoid arthritis. The diffuse nature of the redness and the specific 'boring' quality of the pain make scleritis more likely in this context.

Keratoconjunctivitis sicca
Keratoconjunctivitis sicca (dry eye syndrome) is extremely common in patients with rheumatoid arthritis, often as part of secondary Sjögren's syndrome. It causes chronic ocular irritation, a gritty or foreign body sensation, and can lead to a red eye. However, it does not cause the acute, severe, deep-seated pain described by this patient. While it is a very common comorbidity, it does not fit the acute and severe presentation in the vignette.

Infective keratitis
Infective keratitis is inflammation of the cornea, which is a serious cause of a painful red eye and visual loss. Patients on immunosuppressive therapy for rheumatoid arthritis are at an increased risk of infections. However, keratitis is most commonly associated with contact lens wear or ocular trauma, neither of which are mentioned here. The inflammation is primarily corneal, often with a visible opacity or ulcer, rather than the diffuse scleral injection described.

stem: A 65-year-old male who has a new diagnosis of giant cell arteritis has had a positive relative afferent pupillary defect (RAPD) in his left eye on examination. Which of the following describes the finding of RAPD in this man?
options: The right eye appears to dilate when light is shone on the right eye
The left eye appears to dilate when light is shone on the left eye
The left and right eye appears to dilate when light is shone on the left eye
The left and right eye appears to dilate when light is shone on the right eye
The left and right eye appears to constrict when light is shone on the left eye
explanation:
The left and right eye appears to dilate when light is shone on the left eye
A relative afferent pupillary defect is when the affected and normal eye appears to dilate when light is shone on the affected eye. This leads to reduced constriction, hence appears as dilation, of both pupils when light is shone from the unaffected eye to the affected eye.

The right eye appears to dilate when light is shone on the right eye
The right eye appears to dilate when light is shone on the right eye. This is incorrect because in RAPD, both eyes appear to dilate when light is shone on the affected eye, not the unaffected eye.

The left eye appears to dilate when light is shone on the left eye
The left eye appears to dilate when light is shone on the left eye. This is incorrect because in RAPD, both eyes appear to dilate when light is shone on the affected eye, not just the affected eye.

The left and right eye appears to dilate when light is shone on the right eye
The left and right eye appears to dilate when light is shone on the right eye. This is incorrect because in RAPD, both eyes appear to dilate when light is shone on the affected eye, not the unaffected eye.

The left and right eye appears to constrict when light is shone on the left eye
The left and right eye appears to constrict when light is shone on the left eye. This is incorrect because in RAPD, both eyes appear to dilate, not constrict, when light is shone on the affected eye.

stem: A 55-year-old woman attends the clinic with worsening vision. She has a past medical history of poorly controlled diabetes mellitus. A slit lamp examination confirms proliferative diabetic retinopathy. You counsel the patient for panretinal laser photocoagulation. What complication is this patient most at risk of?
explanation:
Reduction of the visual field
Following panretinal laser photocoagulation up to 50% of patients have a noticeable reduction in their visual field. This is a common complication following panretinal laser photocoagulation with up to 50% of patients having a noticeable reduction in their visual field.

Endophthalmitis
Endophthalmitis is incorrect. Endophthalmitis is not a recognised complication of panretinal laser photocoagulation.

Macular oedema
Macular oedema is incorrect. Whilst this can occur, it is a rare complication.

Myopia
Myopia is incorrect. Myopia is not a recognised complication of panretinal laser photocoagulation.

Vitreous haemorrhage
Vitreous haemorrhage is incorrect. Whilst this can occur, it is a rare complication.

stem: A 64-year-old man with a 20-year history of type 2 diabetes mellitus is seen in clinic with worsening vision over the last 8 months. Visual acuity is reduced, and fundoscopy shows numerous microaneurysms, blot haemorrhages, hard exudates, and evidence of neovascularisation. He is recommended to undergo pan-retinal laser photocoagulation as part of his treatment. Which option is a potential complication of the procedure?
explanation:
Decrease in night vision
A decrease in night vision is a potential complication of panretinal photocoagulation. PRP destroys peripheral photoreceptors responsible for scotopic (night) vision, leading to decreased night vision as a common complication.

Corneal scarring
Corneal scarring is incorrect as PRP does not involve the cornea. It involves applying laser burns to the retinal surface to reduce neovascularisation, and so, it does not cause damage to the corneal tissue. Corneal scarring may instead occur in anterior segment surgery, corneal trauma, or infection.

Endophthalmitis
Endophthalmitis is incorrect as PRP does not involve breaching the globe or introducing pathogens into the intraocular space, making the risk of endophthalmitis low. Endophthalmitis may instead occur if the patient has undergone intraocular surgery, such as vitrectomy or procedures like intravitreal injections, where there is a risk of direct pathogen entry into the eye.

Optic disc swelling
Optic disc swelling is incorrect as PRP is not known to cause optic nerve oedema. It targets the peripheral retina to reduce neovascularisation, without directly affecting the optic nerve head. Optic disc swelling is instead caused by conditions leading to raised intracranial pressure (papilloedema) or optic neuritis.

Retinal vein occlusion
Retinal vein occlusion is incorrect (RVO) as PRP is not known to cause RVO. PRP mainly targets the peripheral retina to reduce ischaemia and neovascularisation without causing venous thrombosis or obstruction. However, RVO can be caused by diabetes mellitus itself, hypertension, and hypercoagulable states (e.g. malignancy).

stem: A 68-year-old woman with dry age-related macular degeneration is reviewed by her ophthalmologist with slowly progressive central visual distortion in both eyes. She has a 50-pack-year history of smoking, and continued to smoke 10 per day. What best explains the role of smoking in the pathogenesis of her condition?
explanation:
Increased oxidative stress
Increased oxidative stress is the correct answer. The progressive bilateral central visual distortion and history of dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) point towards a progression of her disease. Smoking is one of the most important risk factors in the development of AMD, and is mediated via direct oxidation. Tobacco smoke introduces free radicals that directly damage retinal pigment epithelium (RPE), which accelerates drusen formation and RPE dysfunction. Oxidative stress is responsible for many health consequences associated with smoking, including cardiovascular disease, increased risk of neoplasm and smoking-related lung damage.

Impaired retinal perfusion
Impaired retinal perfusion is incorrect. Although smoking can affect vascular health, impaired retinal perfusion is more typical of vascular occlusions or diabetic retinopathy. Perfusion is usually preserved in dry AMD until late stages. Additionally, the gradual bilateral central distortion points to degenerative rather than ischaemic pathology.

Increased lutein levels
Increased lutein levels is incorrect. Lutein is a protective macular pigment with antioxidant properties. Therefore, increased lutein will be protective against pathologies such as macular degeneration. Smoking reduces, not increases, lutein levels.

Increased retinal vascular resistance
Increased retinal vascular resistance is incorrect. This is more relevant to hypertensive or arteriolar retinal disease, and tends to result in asymmetrical, patchy changes to peripheral vision or retinal oedema. Therefore, this does not explain the slowly progressive central vision loss.

Interference with macular photopigment regeneration
Interference with macular photopigment regeneration is incorrect. This would be in keeping with vitamin A deficiency or inherited retinal dystrophies. Smoking is not a culprit in altering the visual cycle, but rather causes disruption of oxidative and inflammatory pathways.

stem: Which one of the following causes of Horner's syndrome is due to a lesion in the post-ganglionic part of the nerve supply?
explanation:
Internal carotid aneurysm
The correct answer is Internal carotid aneurysm. Horner's syndrome results from interruption of the sympathetic nerve supply to the eye and can occur at different anatomical levels. An internal carotid artery aneurysm affects the post-ganglionic sympathetic fibers that travel along the internal carotid artery after they have passed through the superior cervical ganglion. This causes the classic triad of ptosis, miosis, and anhidrosis on the affected side.

Stroke
Stroke typically affects the central (first-order) neurons in the hypothalamus or brainstem, representing a central cause of Horner's syndrome rather than a post-ganglionic lesion.

Syringomyelia
Syringomyelia affects the pre-ganglionic (second-order) neurons in the spinal cord, typically at the C8-T2 level. This represents another central cause rather than a post-ganglionic lesion.

Pancoast's tumour
Pancoast's tumor affects the pre-ganglionic sympathetic fibers as they exit the spinal cord and travel through the thoracic apex, before reaching the superior cervical ganglion. This is therefore a pre-ganglionic rather than post-ganglionic cause.

Thyroidectomy
Thyroidectomy can cause Horner's syndrome by damaging the cervical sympathetic chain during surgery, which contains pre-ganglionic fibers. This represents another pre-ganglionic cause rather than a postganglionic lesion.

stem: A 68-year-old woman presents to the Emergency Department with a 3-hour history of a severe, right-sided headache and vomiting. Her symptoms started whilst watching a film in a dimly lit room. She reports seeing haloes around lights and wears glasses for reading. On examination, her right eye is red, with a hazy cornea and a fixed, semidilated pupil. What is the most appropriate initial management?
explanation:
Intravenous acetazolamide
Intravenous acetazolamide is the most appropriate initial management. Acetazolamide is a carbonic anhydrase inhibitor that rapidly reduces the production of aqueous humour by the ciliary body. This leads to a significant and swift reduction in IOP. It is administered systemically (usually intravenously) to achieve a rapid onset of action in the acute setting. It is a cornerstone of initial medical therapy and is typically given alongside a combination of topical agents while awaiting urgent ophthalmology review for definitive treatment (laser peripheral iridotomy).

Intravenous mannitol
Intravenous mannitol is an osmotic diuretic that can also be used to rapidly lower IOP by dehydrating the vitreous humour. However, it is generally considered a second-line agent, reserved for cases where the IOP is extremely high or does not respond to initial treatment with acetazolamide and topical agents. Its use is also more complex, with potential for significant fluid shifts and electrolyte disturbances, making acetazolamide the preferred initial systemic therapy.

Topical pilocarpine
Topical pilocarpine is a miotic agent that constricts the pupil. This action helps to pull the peripheral iris away from the trabecular meshwork, physically opening the drainage angle. While it is an important part of the treatment for AACG, it is not the best initial step. If the IOP is very high (e.g., > 40-50 mmHg), the iris sphincter can become ischaemic and will not respond to pilocarpine. Therefore, it is typically administered only after the IOP has started to decrease following systemic therapy with acetazolamide.

Topical timolol
Topical timolol is a beta-blocker eye drop that reduces the production of aqueous humour. It is a key component of the topical therapy for AACG and is usually administered promptly. However, in a patient with such severe symptoms indicative of a very high IOP, systemic treatment with intravenous acetazolamide is the most crucial initial step to gain rapid control of the pressure. Topical therapy alone is often insufficient in the acute phase.

Urgent CT head
An Urgent CT head would be a reasonable consideration in a patient presenting with a sudden severe headache and vomiting, as it is important to rule out intracranial pathology like a subarachnoid haemorrhage. However, in this case, the presence of clear and specific unilateral ocular signs (red eye, hazy cornea, fixed semi-dilated pupil) and visual symptoms (haloes) makes AACG the definitive diagnosis. Proceeding directly to a CT scan would inappropriately delay sight-saving treatment.

stem: A 56-year-old female with longstanding rheumatoid arthritis presented to her general practitioner with redness of her right eye. She reports feeling slight discomfort and being irritating with occasional watering of the eye. She denied any dryness or pain as such. Assessment of her pupils was normal and light did not cause her any discomfort. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Episcleritis
Episcleritis is one of the many ocular manifestations of rheumatoid arthritis. In episcleritis, the episclera becomes inflamed and red. It often causes irritation, soreness or a gritty sensation but importantly no pain.

Corneal ulceration
Corneal ulceration is a painful sore that develops on the outer surface of your eye. They're more common in contact lens wearers.

Keratitis
Keratitis is marked by moderate to intense pain and usually involves impaired eyesight, photophobia, redness of the eye with a gritty sensation.

Keratoconjunctivitis sicca
Keratoconjunctivitis sicca is dryness of the conjunctiva and cornea. Too few tears may be produced, or tears may evaporate too quickly. There is no evidence to suggest this occurring here.

Scleritis
Scleritis is painful, episcleritis is not painful. Scleritis is a disorder in which the sclera becomes severely inflamed and red. It can be very painful. Given the absence of pain, in this case, scleritis is unlikely.

stem: A 53-year-old male who presents to the emergency department with a painful red eye. He has vomited once since the pain started. He reports seeing haloes around lights. His immediate management includes latanoprost and pilocarpine, and he requires an urgent ophthalmology referral. What is the mode of the action of pilocarpine?
explanation:
Muscarinic receptor agonist
Pilocarpine is a muscarinic receptor agonist - it increases uveoscleral outflow by constricting the pupil.

Muscarinic receptor antagonist
Examples of muscarinic receptor antagonists include atropine and hyoscine (scopolamine) - these are not used in the management of glaucoma.

Nicotinic receptor agonist
Nicotinic receptor agonists include nicotine and acetylcholine, therefore this answer is incorrect.

Nicotinic receptor antagonist
Nicotinic receptor antagonists include succinylcholine, atracurium, vecuronium and bupropion.

Adrenergic receptor agonist
Adrenergic receptor agonists include norepinephrine and epinephrine.

stem: A 52-year-old woman is referred to the ophthalmology clinic by her optician. The optician detected raised intraocular pressure (IOP) in both eyes. The patient is currently asymptomatic but describes a family history of glaucoma. She has no other past medical history of note. On examination, the IOP is currently 23 mmHg bilaterally. The ophthalmologist prescribes latanoprost eye drops to be used daily in both eyes. What is the mechanism of action of this drug?
options: Reduces aqueous production and increases uveoscleral outflow
explanation:
Increases uveoscleral outflow
Latanoprost is a prostaglandin analog used in glaucoma. It works by increasing uveoscleral outflow. Latanoprost is a prostaglandin analogue and is commonly used first-line in patients with open-angle glaucoma. It acts by increasing uveoscleral outflow. It is typically administered once daily. Side effects include brown pigmentation of the iris and increased eyelash length.

Increases choroidal blood flow
Oral acetazolamide appears to increase choroidal blood flow in some studies. Latanoprost does not cause this effect.

Increases intravascular osmolarity
Oral hyperosmotic drugs such as mannitol may be given in emergencies relating to acute IOP increases. These act by increasing intravascular osmolarity and drawing fluid out of the vitreous humour of the eye. Latanoprost does not act by this mechanism.

Reduces aqueous production
Beta-blockers, such as timolol, are often used in the treatment of glaucoma. They act by reducing aqueous production. Latanoprost does not work via this mechanism.

Reduces aqueous production and increases uveoscleral outflow
Sympathomimetics, such as brimonidine, act by both increasing uveoscleral outflow and reducing aqueous production. Latanoprost only acts via the former mechanism, not the latter.

stem: A 45-year-old female known to have rheumatoid arthritis presents to the hospital's emergency department with a red, swollen painful right eye. The patient is currently on hydroxychloroquine, with good drug compliance. She has had 3 arthritic flares in the past year, all responding to the IV steroids. She frequently takes artificial teardrops, with good effect, as she often experiences foreign body sensation. However, her current ocular symptoms are not in keeping with previous episodes and are not responding to artificial teardrops. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Scleritis
Scleritis is characterised by a red, swollen, and painful eye as described in this patient.

Allergic conjunctivitis
As there is no clear history of stimuli exposure (i.e. pollen, dust) or increased lacrimation allergic conjunctivitis is least likely in this case.

Episcleritis
Episcleritis is commonly mistaken for scleritis however, episcleritis is painless.

Keratitis
Keratitis is usually associated with eye discharge.

Retinopathy
Retinopathy can occur due to hydroxychloroquine use in rheumatoid arthritis therefore, annual eye exams are advised for rheumatoid patients. Retinopathy results in a painless reduction in visual acuity which is not in keeping with this patient's presentation.

stem: A 22-year-old woman presented with a history of a sudden loss of vision of her left eye for 4 days in duration. It was associated with pain in eye movement. Ocular examination revealed visual acuity of the left eye was only counting fingers with a positive afferent pupillary defect. Visual acuity of the right eye was 6/6. Anterior segments of both eyes showed normal ocular findings. The contrast sensitivity and colour vision test were severely impaired. The visual field showed unilateral central scotoma. What is the underlying diagnosis?
explanation:
Optic neuritis
A central scotoma is a feature of optic neuritis. Optic neuritis is an inflammation of the eye's optic nerve. The two most common symptoms of optic neuritis are vision loss and eye pain. Central scotoma is recognised as a characteristic visual field defect pattern of optic neuritis. It may be associated with demyelinating diseases or infectious or inflammatory processes. The signs include decreased visual acuity, decreased colour vision (red desaturation) and relative afferent pupillary defect (RAPD).

Corneal ulceration
Corneal ulceration is an erosion or open sore on the surface of the cornea which causes sudden painful visual loss. A corneal ulcer usually results from an eye infection, but severe dry eye or other eye disorders can cause it. The absence of tearing and redness make this diagnosis unlikely.

Episcleritis
Episcleritis is a common condition affecting the episclera, the layer of tissue between the surface membrane (conjunctiva) and the firm white part of the eye (the sclera). In episcleritis, the episclera becomes inflamed and red. It often causes irritation, soreness or a gritty sensation. However, it typically does not cause visual loss which makes this incorrect.

Glaucoma
Glaucoma is an eye condition that is often associated with elevated intraocular pressure, in which damage to the optic nerve can lead to loss of vision and even blindness. The visual field loss (scotoma) in glaucoma has a distinctive pattern that differs from visual loss due to other causes and includes para-central scotoma, nasal step, and arcuate defect.

Macular degeneration
Macular degeneration produces a scotoma which most often appears in the central visual field resulting in its being called a central scotoma. In dry macular degeneration, the light-sensing cells (called rods and cones) in the centre of the retina degenerate along with their supporting cells. This diagnosis is unlikely as it is typically painless and also age-related.

stem: A 76-year-old man attends the diabetic eye clinic. He has proliferative retinopathy without vitreous haemorrhage and is being consented to the first-line procedure. What should he be told occurs in up to 50% of patients who have this procedure?
explanation:
A reduction in visual fields
Following panretinal laser photocoagulation up to 50% of patients have a noticeable reduction in their visual field. Panretinal laser photocoagulation is the first-line procedure for proliferative retinopathy. Due to the retinal scarring caused by this procedure, there is a 50% chance of a reduction in visual fields. This procedure is often used in combination with intravitreal VEGF.

Brown pigmentation of the iris
Brown pigmentation of the iris is incorrect. This is a side effect of prostaglandin analogues, given for open-angle glaucoma.

Corneal scarring
Corneal scarring is incorrect. This is a complication of keratitis.

Increased intraocular pressure
There is a high chance of rising intraocular pressure is incorrect. This is a common complication of laser peripheral iridotomy, the definitive management for acute angle-closure glaucoma.

Vitreous detachment
Vitreous detachment is incorrect. This is a condition associated with near-sightedness and ageing.

stem: A 25-year-old woman attends the emergency department with a gradual loss of vision in her left eye. She explains this has been progressing over the last couple of days. She is not experiencing any black spots or curtain-like sensations in her vision. On examination, there is pain in eye movement, with a relative afferent pupillary defect and central scotoma. Given the likely diagnosis, what else would be expected in her presentation?
explanation:
Poor discrimination of colour
Colour vision ('red desaturation') is affected in optic neuritis. Poor discrimination of colour is the correct answer. The diagnosis described in this patient is optic neuritis. This is inflammation of the optic nerve due to multiple sclerosis, diabetes or syphilis. As described, optic neuritis will present with gradual loss of visual acuity, painful eye movements, a relative afferent pupillary defect, and evidence of a central scotoma. Another important feature of optic neuritis is affected colour vision and red desaturation of images.

Jaw claudication
Jaw claudication is incorrect. This would be seen classically in a diagnosis of temporal arteritis. Although this would also present with visual loss and a relative afferent pupillary defect due to an affected optic nerve as described in this vignette, patients typically do not describe a central scotoma. They also may describe a severe unilateral headache over the temporal region which is not seen in this patient, and patients are often older on initial presentation.

Optic disc cupping
Optic disc cupping is incorrect. This can be seen in a diagnosis of primary open-angle glaucoma. Although patients can also describe a gradual visual loss as seen in this patient, they typically have a loss of the peripheral fields of vision, as opposed to the development of a central scotoma that is described in this vignette.

Ptosis
Ptosis is incorrect. This is seen in a variety of conditions some of which include a third nerve palsy and myasthenia gravis. Given the most likely diagnosis in this vignette is optic neuritis due to this patient's presentation, ptosis is not the most appropriate answer as this is not seen in cases of optic neuritis.

Symptoms worse in the dark
Symptoms worse in the dark is incorrect. Although symptoms may be worse in the dark this is not a characteristic feature seen in optic neuritis. This presenting feature can be seen in retinitis pigmentosum, a genetic disorder that leads to loss of night vision and peripheral vision.

stem: A 52-year-old male is admitted to the acute medical admissions unit with a 1-day history of a left-sided headache, retro-orbital pain, and dull left-sided facial pain. He has a history of hypertension and migraine and takes ramipril 2.5mg. On examination, he has a partial ptosis and enophthalmos of the left eye. Pupil examination demonstrates anisocoria with miosis of the left eye. His visual acuity is 6/6 bilaterally and the remainder of neurological examination is normal with normal sweating bilaterally. What is the single most likely cause of these symptoms?
explanation:
Carotid artery dissection
Carotid artery dissection typically presents with ipsilateral pain and in this case, it was the cause of a partial Horner's syndrome with ipsilateral ptosis and miosis, in the absence of anhidrosis. Although Horner's syndrome is an uncommon presentation of carotid artery dissection, it is documented in case reports and important to recognise to avoid further neurological consequences such as an ischaemic stroke.

Cervical rib
A cervical rib or Pancoast tumour cause pre-ganglionic interruption of the sympathetic chain. In addition to ptosis and miosis, they would cause anhidrosis of just the face.

Pancoast's tumour
A cervical rib or Pancoast tumour cause pre-ganglionic interruption of the sympathetic chain. In addition to ptosis and miosis, they would cause anhidrosis of just the face.

Stroke
A stroke or syringomyelia are central lesions. If they caused a Horner's syndrome then in addition to ptosis and miosis, there would be anhidrosis of the head, arm, and trunk.

Syringomyelia
A stroke or syringomyelia are central lesions. If they caused a Horner's syndrome then in addition to ptosis and miosis, there would be anhidrosis of the head, arm, and trunk.

stem: A 68-year-old man with a history of type 2 diabetes mellitus presents with worsening eye sight. Mydriatic drops are applied and fundoscopy reveals pre-proliferative diabetic retinopathy. A referral to ophthalmology is made. Later in the evening whilst driving home he develops pain in his left eye associated with decreased visual acuity. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Acute angle closure glaucoma
Acute angle closure glaucoma is the correct diagnosis in this scenario. The use of mydriatic drops in a predisposed individual can precipitate acute angle closure glaucoma by dilating the pupil, which causes the peripheral iris to bunch up and block the drainage angle of the anterior chamber. This patient's age and the sudden onset of eye pain with decreased visual acuity following pupillary dilation are classical features. This is an ophthalmic emergency requiring immediate treatment to prevent permanent vision loss.

Keratitis secondary to mydriatic drops
Keratitis secondary to mydriatic drops is incorrect because whilst mydriatic drops can occasionally cause irritation, they do not typically cause keratitis. Furthermore, keratitis usually presents with symptoms of foreign body sensation, photophobia, and watering rather than acute severe pain and sudden visual loss.

Proliferative diabetic retinopathy
Proliferative diabetic retinopathy is incorrect because whilst this patient has pre-proliferative changes and may progress to proliferative disease, this progression occurs gradually over weeks to months rather than acutely. Additionally, proliferative changes alone would not typically cause acute pain.

Central retinal artery occlusion
Central retinal artery occlusion is incorrect because whilst this condition causes sudden visual loss, it is typically painless. It also presents with a characteristic cherry-red spot at the macula and pale retina on fundoscopy, which would have been noted during the earlier examination.

Vitreous haemorrhage
Vitreous haemorrhage is incorrect because although it can occur in diabetic retinopathy and cause sudden visual loss, it is typically painless. Patients usually describe seeing floaters or a sudden onset of 'cobwebs' or darkness in their vision, rather than the acute pain described in this scenario.

stem: A 74-year-old man presents to ophthalmology clinic after seeing his optician. They have noticed raised intra-ocular pressure and decreased peripheral vision. His past medical history includes asthma and type 2 diabetes mellitus. What is the most appropriate treatment given the likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Latanoprost
The correct answer is Latanoprost. This patient's presentation of raised intraocular pressure and decreased peripheral vision suggests a diagnosis of open-angle glaucoma, which is the most common form of glaucoma. Latanoprost is a prostaglandin analogue and it works by increasing the outflow of aqueous humour from the eye, thereby reducing intraocular pressure. Prostaglandin analogues such as latanoprost are first-line treatments for open-angle glaucoma.

Pilocarpine
Pilocarpine is incorrect because it is not a first-line treatment for open-angle glaucoma in the UK. Pilocarpine is a muscarinic receptor agonist that increases the outflow of aqueous humour but has more side effects than latanoprost, including miosis (pupil constriction) and potential worsening of presbyopia.

Timolol
Timolol would not be an appropriate choice for this patient due to his past medical history of asthma. Timolol is a non-selective beta-blocker which can cause bronchoconstriction and potentially exacerbate asthma symptoms.

Dorzolamide
Dorzolamide is also incorrect. Dorzolamide is a carbonic anhydrase inhibitor used as adjunctive therapy in patients with inadequate response to first-line treatments or if they are intolerant to them. It works by reducing production of aqueous humour but it's less effective than latanoprost.

Brimonidine
Brimonidine would not be the best choice either. Brimonidine is an alpha-2 adrenergic receptor agonist that reduces the production of aqueous humour and increases its outflow. However, it has more systemic side effects compared to latanoprost and like dorzolamide, brimonidine would only be considered if first-line treatments were ineffective or not tolerated.

stem: A 78-year-old woman is referred to the ophthalmology clinic with a six-month history of progressively worsening vision. She struggles to read the newspaper and recognise faces, but reports her peripheral vision is unaffected. She has a 40-pack-year smoking history. On examination, her visual acuity is 6/24 in both eyes. What is the most likely finding on fundoscopy?
options: Flame haemorrhages and cotton wool spots
explanation:
Drusen in the macular region
Elderly patient, gradual, central visual loss → age-related macular degeneration. The correct answer is Drusen in the macular region. This patient's presentation is highly suggestive of dry age-related macular degeneration (ARMD). The key features are her advanced age, the gradual onset of symptoms over several months, and the specific nature of her visual loss, which is central (affecting detailed tasks like reading and recognising faces) while sparing the periphery. Smoking is a major modifiable risk factor for ARMD. Fundoscopy in dry ARMD characteristically reveals drusen, which are yellow-white deposits of extracellular material located between Bruch's membrane and the retinal pigment epithelium. These deposits accumulate in the macular region, disrupting photoreceptor function and leading to the classic central scotoma. While these changes are often bilateral, they can be asymmetrical. The diagnosis is clinical, based on the history and fundoscopic findings.

Cupping of the optic disc
Cupping of the optic disc is the hallmark sign of glaucomatous optic neuropathy. Primary open-angle glaucoma is a common cause of progressive, irreversible visual loss in the elderly. However, it classically causes a gradual loss of peripheral vision, often going unnoticed by the patient until it is advanced, leading to 'tunnel vision'. The patient in this scenario explicitly states her peripheral vision is unaffected, and her symptoms are of central visual loss, making glaucoma a less likely diagnosis.

Flame haemorrhages and cotton wool spots
Flame haemorrhages and cotton wool spots are characteristic findings of hypertensive or diabetic retinopathy. These signs indicate microvascular damage within the retina. While these conditions are prevalent in this age group, the patient's symptoms are specifically localised to the macula. Retinopathy typically causes more diffuse visual disturbance or can lead to macular oedema, but the classic presentation described here points away from a primary vasculopathy and towards a degenerative process centred on the macula.

Neovascularisation of the optic disc
Neovascularisation of the optic disc is a feature of proliferative retinopathy, most commonly seen in advanced diabetic retinopathy or following a central retinal vein occlusion. It represents the eye's response to widespread retinal ischaemia. While neovascularisation is a feature of 'wet' ARMD, it occurs in the choroid beneath the macula (choroidal neovascularisation), not typically at the optic disc. The gradual, six-month history is also more in keeping with dry ARMD than the more acute visual loss associated with proliferative disease.

Pale, swollen optic disc
Pale, swollen optic disc is indicative of optic disc oedema. In this age group, this finding would raise suspicion of anterior ischaemic optic neuropathy (AION), particularly giant cell arteritis. However, AION typically presents with acute, painless, and often profound visual loss, frequently with an altitudinal field defect. The subacute, progressive, and centrally-focused visual decline over six months described in the scenario is not typical for AION.

stem: A 66-year-old male is referred to ophthalmology by his general practitioner with a complaint of gradual deterioration of peripheral vision bilaterally. His past medical history includes hypertension and a left knee replacement. He is on regular amlodipine. He does not smoke or drink and is retired and lives alone. On examination, there is clinical evidence of a mild reduction in the peripheral vision bilaterally. Formal tonometry demonstrates a raised intraocular pressure of 25 mmHg. Based on the likely diagnosis, the treating ophthalmologist prescribes a medication that works by reducing aqueous production without increasing uveoscleral outflow. Which class of medication has this mechanism of action?
explanation:
Timolol
Beta blockers such as timolol work in primary open-angle glaucoma by reducing aqueous production. The diagnosis is open-angle glaucoma as evidenced by the impaired peripheral vision and raised intraocular pressure.

Brimonidine
The diagnosis is open-angle glaucoma as evidenced by impaired peripheral vision and raised intraocular pressure. Sympathomimetics (e.g. brimonidine, an alpha2-adrenoceptor agonist) work in open-angle glaucoma by both increasing uveoscleral outflow and reducing aqueous production rather than reducing aqueous production, alone.

Ciclosporin
This is not a treatment for open-angle glaucoma but is used topically in severe keratitis in dry eye disease that has not responded to treatment with tear substitutes. It works by inhibiting the production and release of cytokines.

Latanoprost
Prostaglandin analogues are the first-line treatment of open-angle glaucoma but they work by increasing uveoscleral outflow.

Pilocarpine
Miotics (e.g. pilocarpine, a muscarinic receptor agonist) work in open-angle glaucoma by increasing uveoscleral outflow.

stem: A 43-year-old man attends his GP with pain and facial swelling after an upper respiratory tract infection. On examination, erythema and swelling surround the right eye and there is pain on eye movements. Visual acuity is 6/6 on the left and 6/24 on the right. What is the most appropriate course of action?
options: Admit to hospital for IV antibiotics
Prescribe high-dose oral steroids and check thyroid function
Prescribe high-dose oral steroids and refer urgently to Rheumatology
Urgent referral to maxillofacial surgeons for debridement
explanation:
Admit to hospital for IV antibiotics
Patients with orbital cellulitis require admission to hospital for IV antibiotics due to the risk of cavernous sinus thrombosis and intracranial spread. The correct answer is admit to hospital for IV antibiotics. The symptoms described are suggestive of orbital cellulitis. This usually results from the spread of organisms from the upper respiratory tract. Admission for IV antibiotics is recommended as under-treatment can lead to cavernous sinus thrombosis.

Prescribe high-dose oral steroids and check thyroid function
Prescribe high-dose oral steroids and check thyroid function is incorrect. Thyroid eye disease could cause orbital pain and painful eye movements and should be in the differential here. However, the recent upper respiratory tract symptoms and facial pain/swelling are more suggestive of orbital cellulitis, which often results from the spread of infection from the upper respiratory tract.

Prescribe high-dose oral steroids and refer urgently to Rheumatology
Prescribe high-dose oral steroids and refer to Rheumatology is incorrect. This would be the appropriate choice for suspected giant cell arteritis. This condition is extremely unusual under the age of 65. It can cause headache and visual loss but this is usually in the form of monocular blindness rather than reduced acuity.

Supportive management and nasal decongestants
Supportive management and nasal decongestants is incorrect. This would be appropriate for conditions such as sinusitis that may lead to orbital cellulitis. However, the facial pain and swelling with painful eye movements suggest orbital cellulitis has now developed. At this stage, supportive therapy would not be appropriate and IV antibiotics are required.

Urgent referral to maxillofacial surgeons for debridement
Urgent referral to maxillofacial surgeons for debridement is incorrect. Orbital cellulitis is generally managed with IV antibiotics rather than operative intervention. This may be required if there were suspicion of necrotising infection but there is nothing to suggest this is a concern here.

stem: A 24-year-old man attends the emergency department with left eye swelling and painful eye movements. He is usually fit and well with a past medical history of chronic sinusitis only. On examination, his left eye is swollen shut with marked eyelid oedema and erythema that extends from the maxilla up to the eyebrow. When the eye is manually opened there is chemosis. What would the most appropriate initial treatment be for this patient?
explanation:
Intravenous antibiotics
Patients with orbital cellulitis require admission to hospital for IV antibiotics due to the risk of cavernous sinus thrombosis and intracranial spread. This patient has evidence of orbital cellulitis which necessitates urgent treatment with intravenous antibiotics due to the risk to sight and risk of spread. Intravenous antibiotics are the most important part of the initial treatment for orbital cellulitis to treat the underlying infection. If there is evidence of intracranial spread or abscess on CT scan the patient may also require external drainage or neurosurgical intervention. Do not delay starting antibiotics whilst awaiting specialist review.

Immediate CT head
Immediate CT head does form part of the management for orbital cellulitis but it is not the initial priority, treatment with antibiotics takes precedence. The reasoning behind doing a CT head is to assess the extent of spread. For pre-septal cellulitis, a CT head is not usually required but may be completed if the diagnosis is uncertain or examination is difficult e.g. due to extreme swelling.

Ophthalmology review
Ophthalmology review is important in the management of orbital cellulitis, these patients are usually managed under the joint care of ENT and ophthalmology. Waiting for or requesting a specialist review, however, should not delay the administration of antibiotics and so is not the priority.

Oral antibiotics
Oral antibiotics wouldn't be appropriate due to the potential severity of this infection. It is recommended that antibiotics are administered via the IV route rather than oral.

Topical chloramphenicol
Topical chloramphenicol would not be sufficient to treat orbital cellulitis, systemic therapy is required to deliver sufficient antibiotics to the area of infection.

stem: A 45-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department following the sudden onset of pain in the right side of his face whilst hammering a nail into the wall. The pain is described as severe and constant. On examination he has a mild right ptosis and small right pupil. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Carotid artery dissection
This patient has Horner's syndrome caused by a carotid artery dissection. This may be caused by relatively benign trauma to the neck such as hyperextension whilst doing DIY.

stem: A 28-year-old woman is referred to the neurology clinic by her optician due to a difference in her pupil size. On examination, her right pupil is 6mm and poorly reactive to light, while the left is 3mm and reacts briskly. When asked to focus on a near object, the right pupil constricts slowly and tonically. Visual acuity is normal. Further examination reveals absent ankle jerks bilaterally. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Holmes-Adie syndrome
Holmes-Adie syndrome is the correct diagnosis. This condition is characterised by the combination of a tonic pupil and absent or reduced deep tendon reflexes. The patient is a young woman, which is the typical demographic. The examination findings for the right eye are classic for a tonic pupil: it is dilated (mydriatic), shows a minimal or absent reaction to light, but demonstrates a slow, sustained (tonic) constriction with near accommodation. This phenomenon is known as light-near dissociation. The pathophysiology involves damage to the ciliary ganglion or postganglionic parasympathetic fibres, leading to denervation of the pupillary sphincter and ciliary muscle. Over time, aberrant reinnervation occurs, particularly from fibres controlling accommodation, explaining the slow response to near vision. The associated areflexia, most commonly affecting the ankle jerks, is thought to result from pathology in the dorsal root ganglia. The condition is typically benign and idiopathic.

Argyll Robertson pupil
Argyll Robertson pupil is an important differential for light-near dissociation, but it is incorrect here. The key difference is the pupil size and shape. Argyll Robertson pupils, classically associated with tertiary syphilis, are typically small (miotic), irregular in shape, and almost always bilateral. The patient in this scenario has a large (mydriatic), regular, and unilateral pupil, which is not consistent with this diagnosis. Therefore, despite the shared feature of light-near dissociation, the overall clinical picture is incompatible with an Argyll Robertson pupil.

Third nerve palsy
Third nerve palsy is a crucial differential for any patient presenting with a unilateral dilated pupil, as it can be caused by a compressive lesion such as a posterior communicating artery aneurysm. However, in this case, it is less likely. A complete third nerve palsy would also present with significant ptosis and ophthalmoplegia, causing the eye to be deviated 'down and out'. While a partial palsy can occur, the slow, tonic nature of the near response is highly characteristic of a Holmes-Adie pupil and not a feature of an acute third nerve palsy. The absence of other neurological signs makes a third nerve palsy less probable.

Horner's syndrome
Horner's syndrome is incorrect as it presents with features opposite to those described. Horner's syndrome is caused by a disruption of the oculosympathetic pathway. This results in the classic triad of miosis (a constricted pupil), partial ptosis, and ipsilateral facial anhidrosis. This patient presents with a dilated pupil (mydriasis), which is a sign of parasympathetic dysfunction, not sympathetic dysfunction. Therefore, Horner's syndrome can be confidently excluded based on the primary examination finding.

Multiple sclerosis
Multiple sclerosis (MS) is a common neurological condition affecting young adults and can present with various ophthalmological signs. However, a tonic pupil is not a characteristic feature of MS. More common findings include optic neuritis, internuclear ophthalmoplegia, or nystagmus. Furthermore, MS is an upper motor neurone disease, which typically causes hyperreflexia. The finding of absent ankle jerks (areflexia) points towards a peripheral neuropathy or ganglionopathy, which is consistent with Holmes-Adie syndrome but not with MS.

stem: A 57-year-old presents to the clinic three weeks after undergoing panretinal photocoagulation (PRP) for proliferative diabetic retinopathy. He reports mild fluctuating visional changes throughout the day and that his peripheral vision seems less clear than before the procedure. He has no pain, redness, or discharge, and his visual acuity is normal on examination. The PRP-treated areas appear to be healing without signs of infection or acute retinal detachment. Intraocular pressure is within normal limits. What is the most likely complication associated with this patient’s symptoms?
explanation:
Reduced rod cell function
A decrease in night vision is a potential complication of panretinal photocoagulation. The patient’s fluctuating visual changes, following PRP, can indicate reduced night vision, a complication caused by reduced rod cell function. Rod cells, concentrated in the peripheral retina, are crucial for adapting to low-light conditions. PRP, designed to treat proliferative diabetic retinopathy by ablating hypoxic peripheral retinal tissue, inadvertently damages rod cells, impairing the retina's ability to adjust to varying light levels. His normal visual acuity during examination is likely due to the well-lit environment, which relies on cone cell function rather than rods. The peripheral vision changes further support PRP-induced damage.

Epiretinal membrane formation
Epiretinal membranes (ERMs) typically cause central visual blurring or distortion, rather than fluctuating vision or reduced night vision. ERMs form at the macula, far from the peripheral retinal tissue targeted by PRP. This patient's fluctuating vision and normal visual acuity in a well-lit clinic argue against ERM-related findings, making it an unlikely diagnosis.

Foveal ischaemia
Foveal ischaemia manifests with central scotomas or blurred central vision and does not cause fluctuating vision or reduced night vision. PRP targets the peripheral retina and spares the macula, making foveal ischaemia improbable in this case. The patient’s stable visual acuity during examination further excludes this as a cause, as the fovea remains functional.

Neovascularisation
Neovascularisation typically presents with symptoms of recurrent proliferative diabetic retinopathy, such as vitreous haemorrhage or increased intraocular pressure. PRP aims to prevent this complication, and the patient’s examination findings of normal intraocular pressure and stable visual acuity suggest neovascularisation is unlikely to explain the symptoms.

Progression of diabetic macular oedema
Diabetic macular oedema primarily causes central vision distortion, not fluctuating vision or reduced night vision. The absence of central vision issues or macular involvement, in this case, makes macular oedema progression unlikely. Additionally, the patient’s normal visual acuity in the clinic supports the exclusion of this diagnosis, as the macula is not significantly affected.

stem: A 71-year-old man presents with severe pain around his right eye and vomiting. On examination the right eye is red and decreased visual acuity is noted. Which one of the following options is the most appropriate initial treatment?
explanation:
Topical pilocarpine + intravenous acetazolamide
Alongside eye drops, IV acetazolamide is used in the initial emergency medical management of acute angle-closure glaucoma. This patient's presentation of severe ocular pain, redness, nausea, vomiting and decreased visual acuity is suggestive of acute angle-closure glaucoma (AACG). The initial management of AACG in the UK involves reducing intraocular pressure rapidly. Topical pilocarpine constricts the pupil and widens the anterior chamber angle, allowing for improved aqueous humour drainage. Intravenous acetazolamide, a carbonic anhydrase inhibitor, reduces the production of aqueous humour in the ciliary body thereby decreasing intraocular pressure.

Topical pilocarpine + oral prednisolone
Topical pilocarpine + oral prednisolone is not the best option as oral prednisolone does not have a role in the initial treatment of AACG. While it can reduce inflammation associated with other eye conditions such as uveitis or optic neuritis, it does not contribute to lowering intraocular pressure.

Topical pilocarpine + topical steroids
Topical pilocarpine + topical steroids is also incorrect for similar reasons. Topical steroids may be used to treat inflammatory conditions of the eye but do not significantly lower intraocular pressure and are therefore not useful in this setting.

Topical steroids
Topical steroids, again, would not be beneficial in this case as they do not contribute to lowering intraocular pressure which is crucial in managing AACG.

Topical steroids + intravenous acetazolamide
Topical steroids + intravenous acetazolamide would partially help by reducing intraocular pressure through IV acetazolamide; however, without topical pilocarpine to constrict the pupil and widen the anterior chamber angle, this combination would be less effective than using both pilocarpine and acetazolamide together.

stem: A 35-year-old man presents with visual problems. He has had very poor vision in the dark for a long time but is now worried as he is developing 'tunnel vision'. He states his grandfather had a similar problem and was registered blind in his 50's. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Retinitis pigmentosa
Retinitis pigmentosa - night blindness + tunnel vision The most likely diagnosis, in this case, is retinitis pigmentosa. Retinitis pigmentosa is a group of inherited retinal disorders characterized by progressive degeneration of the retina, leading to night blindness and peripheral vision loss. The patient's symptoms of poor night vision and developing 'tunnel vision', as well as a family history of visual problems leading to blindness, are classic features of retinitis pigmentosa.

Leber's congenital amaurosis
Leber's congenital amaurosis is an incorrect answer because it presents as severe visual impairment or blindness at birth or within the first few months of life. This condition does not match the patient's age and presentation.

Vitelliform macular dystrophy
Vitelliform macular dystrophy is also an incorrect option. This disorder typically affects central vision due to the accumulation of yellow deposits under the macula, causing distortion or loss of central vision. However, it does not cause night blindness or tunnel vision as described by the patient.

Central serous retinopathy
Central serous retinopathy is another incorrect choice. It usually presents with sudden onset blurred central vision, often affecting only one eye. This condition may resolve spontaneously but can recur in some individuals. It does not cause night blindness or tunnel vision and has no known familial association.

Primary open angle glaucoma
Finally, primary open-angle glaucoma is incorrect as well. Although it can cause tunnel vision due to gradual loss of peripheral vision, primary open-angle glaucoma typically does not cause night blindness. Additionally, this condition usually affects people over 40 years old and has a more insidious onset compared to the patient's presentation.

stem: A 75-year-old man presents with sudden onset of flashes and floaters in his right eye. A systematic enquiry was otherwise unremarkable. He has a past medical history of hypertension. His drug history includes amlodipine. On examination, there is no evidence of visual loss. Ophthalmoscopy is performed: Ophthalmoscopy Features are suggestive of Weiss ring What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Posterior vitreous detachment
Posterior vitreous detachment is correct. The sudden onset of flashers and floaters is most commonly due to a posterior vitreous detachment. It would, of course, be important to consider more serious causes such as retinal detachment. The ophthalmoscopy features of a Weiss ring (peripapillary glial tissue that remains attached to the posterior vitreous cortex following posterior vitreous detachment) adds weight to the diagnosis.

Acute angle-closure glaucoma
Acute angle-closure glaucoma is incorrect. This condition presents with sudden onset of severe unilateral eye pain or a headache associated with blurred vision, rainbow-coloured halos around bright lights, nausea, and vomiting. The absence of any of these features, and the presence of flashes and floaters make acute glaucoma an unlikely diagnosis.

Chorioretinitis
Chorioretinitis is incorrect. This condition usually presents with the sudden onset of flashes, floaters, blurred vision, loss of vision, and scotomas. Chorioretinitis is most commonly infective in origin with toxoplasmosis and cytomegalovirus being the commonest organisms predominantly in immune-deficient patients. The relative rarity of this condition and the absence of immunodeficiency makes this a less likely diagnosis.

Retinal detachment
Retinal detachment is incorrect. This condition presents with sudden onset visual loss, flashers, floaters, and a 'dark curtain'. Flashers and floaters may precede visual loss early in the disease process. The relative rarity of this condition, the absence of visual loss, and the ophthalmoscopy findings make this a less likely diagnosis.

Vitreous haemorrhage
Vitreous haemorrhage is incorrect. Although vitreous haemorrhage can also present with flashers and floaters, the ophthalmoscopy findings make this an unlikely diagnosis. A vitreous haemorrhage should be directly observed in the majority of cases.

stem: A 24-year-old Chinese woman presents to the GP clinic with a three-month history of intermittent headaches, occasional blurring of vision, and nausea. She has a body mass index (BMI) of 21 kg/m². Physical examination reveals diminished deep tendon reflexes in the lower limbs. Her eye movements are normal; however, her left pupil is smaller than her right, with the right measuring 4mm and the left 2.5mm. The right pupil does not react to light but reacts slowly to accommodation. On fundoscopy, she has a normal optic disc. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Argyll-Robertson pupil on the right side
Holmes-Adie pupil on the right side
Left-sided oculomotor nerve palsy due to posterior communicating artery aneurysm
Right-sided oculomotor nerve palsy due to idiopathic intracranial hypertension (IIH)
explanation:
Holmes-Adie pupil on the right side
Holmes-Adie pupil on the right side is the correct answer. The Holmes-Adie pupil predominantly affects females and typically presents as a unilateral dilated pupil (in 80% of cases) that responds poorly to light but may react slowly upon accommodation. It is commonly associated with diminished deep tendon reflexes. Though infrequent, patients may also experience additional symptoms such as headaches, intermittent blurring of vision, nausea, facial pain, and mood swings.

Argyll-Robertson pupil on the right side
Argyll-Robertson pupil on the right side is incorrect because the Argyll-Robertson pupil features pupils that react poorly to light while accommodating well, which is frequently linked with tertiary syphilis. This condition generally manifests commonly in both sides with small pupils, contrasting with the presentation of a single smaller pupil reacting slowly to accommodation as described. Additionally, there is no typical link between Argyll-Robertson pupils and reduced deep tendon reflexes, making this option less likely to be the correct diagnosis.

Left-sided oculomotor nerve palsy due to posterior communicating artery aneurysm
Left-sided oculomotor nerve palsy due to posterior communicating artery aneurysm is incorrect since a classic oculomotor nerve palsy results in a fixed, dilated pupil (mydriasis), potentially accompanied by ptosis and impaired eye movements. The clinical description given of a dilated pupil with poor light reaction and absent leg reflexes does not align with oculomotor nerve palsy. Moreover, an aneurysm affecting the posterior communicating artery would typically precipitate an acute onset of severe headache alongside oculomotor nerve palsy rather than chronic intermittent headaches as depicted in this scenario.

Physiological anisocoria
Physiological anisocoria refers to a benign variation where there is a slight difference in size between both pupils without any other symptoms or neurological findings. It generally does not involve significant differences in the pupils' reactions to light or accommodation. Considering the patient's symptoms of headaches and reduced deep tendon reflexes along with poor pupillary responses, these clinical features suggest a pathological cause rather than physiological variation.

Right-sided oculomotor nerve palsy due to idiopathic intracranial hypertension (IIH)
Right-sided oculomotor nerve palsy due to IIH is incorrect because right-sided oculomotor nerve palsy would typically manifest with pupillary dilation and possibly ptosis or eye movement abnormalities on the affected side. While oculomotor nerve palsy can occur in conjunction with IIH, IIH itself tends to present with early morning headaches that worsen upon straining, blurred vision due to bilateral papilloedema leading to decreased peripheral vision and enlarging blind spots. However, IIH characteristically causes bilateral papilloedema which is not noted in this case. Risk factors for IIH include obesity, being female of childbearing age, and use of oral contraceptives; nonetheless, this patient has a normal BMI and unremarkable optic disc examination findings.

stem: A 64-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes mellitus presents as she has started to bump into things since the morning. Over the previous two days she had noticed some 'floating spots in her eyes'. Examination reveals she has no vision in her right eye. The red reflex on the right side is difficult to elicit and you are unable to visualise the retina on the right side during fundoscopy. Examination of the left fundus reveals changes consistent with pre-proliferative diabetic retinopathy. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Vitreous haemorrhage
The history of diabetes, complete loss of vision in the affected eye and inability to visualise the retina point towards a diagnosis of vitreous haemorrhage.

stem: Which one of the following is least associated with the development of optic atrophy?
explanation:
Zinc deficiency
Zinc deficiency is the least associated with the development of optic atrophy. Zinc plays a crucial role in maintaining the health of the eye and its deficiency can cause symptoms like night blindness or slow wound healing but it doesn't typically lead to optic atrophy.

Tobacco
Tobacco use has been linked to optic atrophy. Tobacco-alcohol amblyopia, also known as toxic amblyopia, is a form of optic neuropathy that can result from tobacco use. It's thought that the toxins in tobacco damage the mitochondria in cells of the optic nerve leading to their dysfunction and subsequent death.

Methanol
Methanol is another substance strongly associated with optic atrophy. Methanol poisoning can cause severe metabolic acidosis and visual disturbances due to its metabolites which are toxic to the retina and optic nerve.

Vitamin B12 deficiency
Vitamin B12 deficiency can also lead to optic atrophy. Vitamin B12 plays an essential role in maintaining the health of nerve cells and the myelin sheath around them. Its deficiency may lead to subacute combined degeneration (SCD) of the spinal cord, peripheral neuropathy and also optic neuropathy causing progressive vision loss leading eventually to optic atrophy if left untreated.

Lead
Exposure to Lead has been found to cause optic atrophy. Lead toxicity can affect many organs including the nervous system where it causes demyelination and axonal damage leading eventually to conditions like peripheral neuropathy or rarely optic atrophy.

stem: Which one of the following is the most common ocular manifestation of rheumatoid arthritis?
explanation:
Keratoconjunctivitis sicca
The correct answer is Keratoconjunctivitis sicca, also known as dry eye syndrome, which affects approximately 15-25% of rheumatoid arthritis (RA) patients. This condition occurs due to autoimmune-mediated inflammation of the lacrimal glands, leading to reduced tear production and subsequent ocular surface damage. It is part of the broader secondary Sjögren's syndrome that frequently accompanies RA. Patients typically present with symptoms including foreign body sensation, burning, and ocular fatigue.

Scleritis
Scleritis is a serious but less common manifestation of RA, affecting only about 1-6% of patients. It presents with severe ocular pain and redness, and while it can be vision-threatening, it is not the most frequently encountered ocular complication in RA patients.

Episcleritis
Episcleritis occurs in approximately 5% of RA patients. While more common than scleritis, it is still less frequent than keratoconjunctivitis sicca. It typically presents as acute onset eye redness without significant pain and is generally self-limiting.

Corneal ulceration
Corneal ulceration is a relatively rare complication of RA. It usually occurs as a secondary complication of severe keratoconjunctivitis sicca or scleritis, rather than as a primary manifestation. It affects less than 1% of RA patients.

Keratitis
Keratitis, while it can occur in RA patients, is not the most common ocular manifestation. It typically develops as a consequence of severe dry eye disease or other primary ocular complications of RA. When it does occur, it's usually in the form of peripheral ulcerative keratitis, but this affects only a small percentage of RA patients.

stem: A 28-year-old woman presents to the eye clinic with sudden, painless loss of vision in her right eye. On examination, visual acuity is reduced on the right. The swinging light test shows that both pupils appear to dilate when a torch is moved from the left to the right eye. Which of the following best explains this clinical finding?
explanation:
Right optic nerve lesion
Relative afferent pupillary defect indicates an optic nerve lesion or severe retinal disease. A relative afferent pupillary defect (RAPD), demonstrated by both pupils appearing to dilate when light is shone in the affected (right) eye during the swinging light test, indicates an abnormality in the afferent limb of the pupillary light reflex pathway. This occurs anterior to the optic chiasm—most commonly due to optic nerve pathology or severe retinal disease in that eye (e.g., optic neuritis). The unaffected left eye's normal response confirms that efferent pathways are intact, making a right-sided pre-chiasmal problem most likely.

Right oculomotor nerve palsy
Right oculomotor nerve palsy would affect the efferent limb of the pupillary reflex on that side, potentially causing a fixed and dilated pupil unresponsive to direct or consensual stimulation. However, it would not cause a relative afferent defect; rather, only one pupil would be abnormal regardless of which eye was stimulated.

Left optic tract lesion
Left optic tract lesion affects fibres after they have crossed at the chiasm and typically results in contralateral homonymous hemianopia rather than an RAPD. Although subtle RAPDs may occur with large postchiasmal lesions due to asymmetric input from crossed fibres, it does not fit this scenario with unilateral vision loss and classic swinging light test findings.

Right homonymous hemianopia
Right homonymous hemianopia describes a visual field defect rather than a specific anatomical lesion; it usually results from damage posterior to the chiasm (optic tract, radiation or occipital cortex) and does not produce an RAPD because both eyes receive equal afferent input.

Bilateral cataracts
Bilateral cataracts, while affecting vision bilaterally by reducing clarity of incoming light, do not selectively impair afferent input enough in one eye alone to produce an RAPD unless extremely asymmetric and dense— which is rare. Cataracts generally do not alter pupillary responses as described here.

stem: A 34-year-old female presents with fatigue and frequent headaches. On examination of her eyes, you notice an abnormality during the swinging light test. As the light is moved from the left to the right eye both pupils appear to dilate. The pupillary response to accommodation is normal bilaterally. Fundoscopy is also normal bilaterally. Her past medical history includes type one diabetes and hypertension. What is the most likely explanation for this patients' signs?
options: Marcus-Gunn Pupil (relative afferent pupillary defect) on the right
Argyll Robertson pupil on the right
explanation:
Marcus-Gunn Pupil (relative afferent pupillary defect) on the right
Marcus Gunn pupil (relative afferent pupillary defect) is diagnosed during the swinging light test. If there is damage to the afferent pathway (retina or optic nerve) of one eye, the pupil of that affected eye will abnormally dilate when a light is shone into it. This is because the consensual pupillary relaxation response from the healthy eye will dominate. Marcus Gunn pupil can be found in patients with multiple sclerosis. Therefore, given the history, this should be ruled out in this patient.

Raised intracranial pressure
The history and examination findings in the question are not typical of raised intracranial pressure. Raised intracranial pressure may present with symptoms such as a headache, vomiting, bilateral blurred vision and seizures. Patients with increased intracranial pressure often have bilateral papilloedema on fundoscopy.

Diabetic eye disease
Although the history states the female is diabetic, there are typically normal pupillary light responses in patients with diabetic eye disease. Furthermore, with diabetic eye disease, you would expect to see some abnormality on fundoscopy.

Holmes-Adie's pupil on the right
Holmes-Adie's pupil is a dilated pupil which poorly (if at all) reacts to direct light, however, slowly reacts to accommodation. This does not correlate to the history.

Argyll Robertson pupil on the right
The information given in the question above does not suggest Argyll Robertson pupil. This is characterised by a constricted pupil that does not respond to light but responds to accommodation. It is usually bilateral and is often associated with neurosyphilis.

stem: A 74-year-old myopic woman with known hypertension presents with a sudden, painless reduction in her vision. She describes a dense shadow obscuring her right eye, this started peripherally and has progressed towards the central vision. On examination, she can only see hand movements in her right eye and has 6/6 visual acuity in her left eye. What is the most likely cause of the loss of vision?
explanation:
Retinal detachment
This case is typical of retinal detachment. It occurs more commonly in people with myopia. It can be preceded by flashes and floaters and tends to present with a shadow to the vision beginning peripherally and progressing centrally.

Central retinal artery occlusion
Central retinal artery occlusion occurs due to a blockage of blood flow from thromboembolism or arteritis. It can cause a partial or complete sudden, painless loss of vision. However, this doesn't tend to occur peripherally and move centrally as described here. Typical features include afferent pupillary defect, 'cherry red' spot on a pale retina.

Central retinal vein occlusion
Central retinal vein occlusion is more common than arterial occlusion and occurs with increasing age, but unlike here is more common in patients with glaucoma. It can cause sudden painless loss of vision in any venous territory and the ophthalmoscope shows severe retinal haemorrhages.

Optic neuritis
Optic neuritis can cause sudden visual loss but this is often transient and associated with painful eye movement.

Vitreous hemorrhage
Vitreous hemorrhage causes a dark spot to a vision where the hemorrhage is rather than a shadow to the vision.

stem: A 32-year-old man presents with night sweats and a cervical lymph node. Aspirate of the node reveals many acid-fast bacilli and PCR confirms the presence of Mycobacterium tuberculosis. He is started on quadruple therapy. As part of the counselling, you warn him of potential side effects including optic neuritis. What symptom should he be warned about?
explanation:
Red desaturation
Colour vision ('red desaturation') is affected in optic neuritis. The anti-tuberculous agent ethambutol can be associated with optic neuritis. This often presents first with deficits in colour vision, particularly red desaturation. In one study, abnormal colour vision was recognised in 94% of patients with optic neuritis.

Diplopia
Diplopia is incorrect. This would be an unusual feature with optic neuritis. It generally occurs with problems of the nerves controlling the extra-ocular muscles, namely III, IV and VI.

Pain relieved by eye movements
Pain relieved by eye movements is incorrect. The opposite is true with optic neuritis, with pain generally exacerbated by eye movements.

Peripheral visual loss
Peripheral visual loss is incorrect. Visual loss in optic neuritis usually represents a central scotoma rather than a peripheral defect.

Sudden monocular blindness
Sudden monocular blindness is incorrect. Complete monocular blindness is unusual in optic neuritis. Where it does occur, the onset is generally gradual rather than sudden.

stem: Which one of the following best describes the action of latanoprost in the management of primary open-angle glaucoma?
explanation:
Increases uveoscleral outflow
Latanoprost is a prostaglandin analogue that works by increasing the uveoscleral outflow of aqueous humour, thereby lowering intraocular pressure. This mechanism of action is particularly effective in the management of primary open-angle glaucoma, where there is an imbalance between aqueous production and drainage.

Carbonic anhydrase inhibitor
Carbonic anhydrase inhibitors such as acetazolamide and dorzolamide are indeed used in the management of glaucoma, but their mechanism of action differs from that of latanoprost. They work by inhibiting carbonic anhydrase in the ciliary body, which reduces the rate of aqueous humour production and thus decreases intraocular pressure.

Reduces aqueous production + increases outflow
This describes the combined actions of two different classes of drugs: beta-blockers (e.g., timolol) which reduce aqueous humour production, and prostaglandin analogues like latanoprost which increase uveoscleral outflow. However, latanoprost does not have any significant effect on aqueous production.

Opens up drainage pores
This could describe trabeculoplasty, a laser treatment for open-angle glaucoma that aims to improve drainage through the trabecular meshwork (the 'drainage pores'). But this does not apply to latanoprost or any other ocular hypotensive medication.

Reduces aqueous production
This would be correct for medications such as beta-blockers or carbonic anhydrase inhibitors but not for latanoprost. As stated earlier, latanoprost works by increasing uveoscleral outflow rather than decreasing aqueous production.

stem: A 25-year-old woman presents to the emergency department with periorbital oedema, erythema, and drainage that is worsening in her left eye. Mild proptosis is seen on examination. A point of care ultrasound is performed to investigate her symptoms further. The modified ocular ultrasound of her left eye demonstrates prominence and oedema of the retro-orbital soft tissue with echogenic fat. What is the management for this patient given the underlying diagnosis?
explanation:
Intravenous antimicrobial
Patients with orbital cellulitis require admission to hospital for IV antibiotics due to the risk of cavernous sinus thrombosis and intracranial spread. Intravenous antimicrobial is required in hospitals for patients with orbital cellulitis due to the risk of cavernous sinus thrombosis and intracranial spread. All patients with a clinical diagnosis of orbital cellulitis MUST be admitted with an ophthalmic opinion sought as soon as possible. Orbital cellulitis is conventionally managed by intravenous antibiotic therapy and is a medical emergency that, if not treated urgently, may lead to blindness and even death.

No antimicrobial
No antimicrobial is inappropriate in this situation given that orbital cellulitis is a medical emergency that, if not treated urgently, may lead to blindness and even death. It necessitates prompt treatment with intravenous antibiotics.

Oral antimicrobial
Oral antimicrobial is not sufficient in this situation. Orbital cellulitis is conventionally managed by intravenous antibiotic therapy and is a medical emergency that, if not treated urgently, may lead to blindness and even death.

Topical antimicrobial
Topical antimicrobial is not sufficient in this situation. Orbital cellulitis is conventionally managed by intravenous antibiotic therapy and is a medical emergency that, if not treated urgently, may lead to blindness and even death.

Topical corticosteroids
Topical corticosteroids are unlikely to be that effective. The use of oral corticosteroids however can help in reducing inflammation with less residual proptosis and restrictions in extraocular movement during recovery. Intravenous antibiotic therapy remains first-line and must be initiated promptly in this medical emergency.

stem: A 67-year-old woman presents for review. She has recently been diagnosed with dry age-related macular degeneration. Which one of the following is the strongest risk factor for developing this condition?
explanation:
Smoking
Smoking is a risk factor for macular degeneration.

Poor diet
Having a balanced diet, with plenty of fresh fruits and vegetables may also slow the progression of macular degeneration.

stem: A 34-year-old female patient is brought into the emergency department by her husband. Husband reports that she has been confused in the last 3 days. She has a long-standing history of severe psoriasis but no other past medical history. Basic observations are all within normal range and a CT head is unremarkable. A fundoscopy reveals bilateral papilloedema. What is the likely cause?
explanation:
Vitamin A toxicity
Vitamin A toxicity is a rare cause of papilloedema. In this case, she is likely to have been taking retinoids for psoriasis.

Encephalitis
Encephalitis does not usually present with papilloedema.

Hydrocephalus
Brain abscess, brain tumour and hydrocephalus are all less likely with a normal CT head.

stem: An 80-year-old male presents to the Neurology clinic with double vision and unsteadiness whilst walking. He has a past medical history of hypertension, hypercholesterolaemia and type 2 diabetes. On examination, you notice a right partial ptosis and miosis. The patient also has notable right facial loss of pain and temperature sensation with left sided truncal sensory loss contralateral to the face. In the clinic, apraclonidine eye drops are added to the affected eye, which causes a dilatation, whilst in the opposite eye, a pupil constriction occurs. After the eye drops have been eliminated from the body, 1% hydroxyamphetamine eye drops are then instilled. One hour after instillation, both pupils dilate. What neurone order is likely affected in the sympathetic pathway?
explanation:
First order
The answer is the first order neurone. Apraclonidine eye drops are initially used to confirm a Horner's pupil. Apraclonidine stimulates both alpha-1 and alpha-2 receptors.
